newsitem.title: CHINA: China listed firms seen in rush to release results.
newsitem.headline: China listed firms seen in rush to release results.

text.p: A rush of results from China's listed companies looms in the final days of April with firms complaining about a shortage of auditors, but analysts said on Tuesday many firms want to hide their poor performance in the avalanche.
With six working days left before the final deadline for reporting 1996 results, only 310 of the 586 companies listed on the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges have issued annual reports for 1996.
It is the belief of the markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen that companies with good results tend to issue their annual reports early, while those with poor results leave them as late as possible.
"Many companies, especially those with poor results, like to report as part of the pack right at the end of the reporting period," said an analyst with a major Chinese brokerage.
"Their hope is that as one of a large group of companies reporting on a given day, they won't receive a lot of attention," he said.
The delays also point to a serious shortage of accountants qualified to do the complex auditing work, made doubly difficult by the relatively messy state of the finances of many Chinese companies.
"One accountant I know is having to audit 20 companies this year," said one analyst. "There are aren't enough qualified accountants in Shanghai to handle the load."
"We have been extremely busy auditing the listed firms' results," said an official at an accounting office in Shenzhen. "There are just too few accounting offices here."

Another reason for the delays, the analysts said, is that China's securities authorities are gradually tightening up the requirements for the annual reports, making the work increasingly time-consuming for accountants and firms alike.

"The China Securities Regulatory Commission had a lot of new requirements for listed companies this year, so the process of doing the annual reports has been much harder," said a broker with a major securities house.
In the past, a much higher degree of flexibility was allowed, with companies often publicly disagreeing with the auditors on the final results.
More than a dozen companies in Shanghai last year had reports in which their auditors reserved judgement on some element of the accounts. So far this year, there has been only one case in Shanghai.
But there is no flexibility on the April 30 deadline, according to the stock exchange authorities.
"Listed firms, under existing rules, must make public their 1996 annual results by the April 30 deadline," said an official at the Shenzhen Securities Management Office.

"We have issued warnings to listed firms based in Shenzhen to release results by the deadline," the official said. "We will impose penalties on companies which delay publishing audited results without a reasonable explanation."
